Paper Videos

TARA learns a single adversarial texture that stays attached to an object and remains effective across different videos, viewpoints, and observation trajectories.

Real-world experiments

We print the learned texture, attach it to real objects, and record videos under changing viewpoints, motion, and occlusion.

Method

One shared texture must work across videos with different content and surface-observation trajectories. Their task gradients can conflict, making direct universal optimization difficult.

TARA uses frame-wise homographies and visibility masks to render the texture along each trajectory, then optimizes it in two stages:

  1. Contrastive alignment. Bring attacked representations from different video–trajectory instances closer together while separating them from their own clean representations.
  2. Task refinement. Starting from the aligned texture, optimize prediction errors with visibility-aware weights. For future frame generation, refine against reconstruction error.

Experimental results

We evaluate action anticipation on EK100, action recognition on SSV2, and future frame generation with DiLA.

Top-1 ASR is conditioned on clean-correct predictions. Avg. is the mean across models.

Generalization across content and trajectories

We evaluate frozen textures without further optimization while changing video content and observation trajectories independently.

Top-1 ASR (%), V-JEPA2-L on EK100. Each condition uses 74 clip instances; unseen content comes from 35 independently captured recordings.

Print–capture robustness

Trajectory benchmark

We annotate surface homographies and visibility masks on EK100 and SSV2, and collect real-world print-and-capture videos. Fixed trajectories allow different textures to be compared under the same geometry and visibility.
